title: The issue resolution process
blurb: State the stages of issue resolution in order, and spot the step that sounds right but isn't one.
question: A bridge repair suffers a failed concrete pour that will delay completion by five weeks, against a two-week tolerance. The project manager has logged it. What are the remaining stages, in order, until the issue is closed?

teach.h: Six stages from problem to closure
teach.body: Once a problem breaches, or is about to breach, tolerance, it follows a set path. Identify and log it; assess its impact; escalate it to the sponsor; agree the resolution and assign actions; apply change control if the resolution changes the baseline; and track the issue to closure, capturing lessons. In plain English: write it down, size it up, take it upstairs, decide, update the plan if needed, and see it through.

teach.body: Escalating a raw problem wastes the sponsor's time and invites a rushed decision. By logging it and assessing its impact first, the project manager arrives with the facts: what happened, what it does to time, cost, quality and scope, and the realistic options. The sponsor can then agree a resolution quickly and confidently. Speed matters, so assessment should be fast, but it still comes first.

children.sub: Update plan, budget or scope formally

teach.caption: Change control keeps every change to the approved baseline authorised and recorded.

items.label: Pour fails test: logged as I-07
Change request: new end date approved

teach.caption: Every stage leaves a record, so the issue log tells the whole story.

teach.h: Closure is a stage, not an afterthought
teach.body: An issue isn't finished when someone says 'sorted'. Tracking to closure means following the agreed actions until the fix is confirmed, recording the outcome and the date, closing the entry in the issue log, and capturing lessons so the next project spots the warning signs earlier. On Westbrook, the lesson was to test concrete supplies before each pour.

teach.h: Is it a stage of issue resolution?
teach.note: Probability scoring belongs to risk analysis: an issue has already happened.

teach.text: 'Share the issue with stakeholders' sounds sensible, and communication does happen throughout, but it is NOT one of the stages. The exam uses it as the odd one out. The stages that sound bureaucratic, 'escalate to the sponsor' and 'apply change control', ARE stages.

items: Stages in order: identify and log, assess impact, escalate to the sponsor, agree the resolution, apply change control, track to closure.
Assess before escalating, so the sponsor decides with the facts.
Change control is applied only if the resolution changes the baseline.
'Share with stakeholders' is NOT a stage.

summary: You can now state the six stages of the issue resolution process in order, say what happens at each, and explain when change control applies. You can also spot 'share the issue with stakeholders' as the distractor.

A.q: What is the first stage of the issue resolution process?
A.why: An issue must first be identified and recorded in the issue log before anything else can happen.

whyNot.0: Escalation comes after the issue has been logged and assessed.
whyNot.2: You can't assess something that hasn't been identified and logged yet.
whyNot.3: Change control comes late, and only if the resolution changes the baseline.

A.q:
Which TWO of the following are stages of the issue resolution process?
1. Assess the impact of the issue.
2. Share the issue with all stakeholders.
3. Agree the resolution.
4. Score the probability of the issue.
A.why: Assessing the impact and agreeing the resolution are both stages of the process.

whyNot.0: Sharing with stakeholders is not a stage of the process.
whyNot.1: Neither is a stage: sharing is the classic distractor and issues have no probability.
whyNot.3: Probability scoring belongs to risks, which are uncertain.

A.q: Which stage comes immediately after escalating the issue to the sponsor?
A.why: Once escalated, the sponsor and PM agree the resolution and assign actions.

whyNot.1: Tracking to closure is the final stage.
whyNot.2: Logging is the very first stage.

B.q: When is change control applied during issue resolution?
options: When the agreed fix changes the baseline
Whenever an issue is first logged by the PM
Only after the issue has been formally closed
Before the issue's impact has been assessed
B.why: Change control is needed when the agreed resolution alters the approved baseline, such as the end date or budget.

whyNot.1: Logging is stage one; change control isn't triggered by logging.
whyNot.2: Change control is applied before closure, while the fix is being put in place.
whyNot.3: Until the impact is assessed and a fix agreed, there is no change to control.

B.q: What happens at the final stage of the issue resolution process?
options: The issue is shared with every stakeholder
The issue is tracked to closure, with lessons
The issue is moved back onto the risk register
The issue is scored for probability and impact
B.why: The final stage tracks the issue until the fix is confirmed, closes it and captures lessons.

whyNot.0: Sharing with stakeholders is not a stage of the process.
whyNot.2: A resolved issue is closed in the issue log; it doesn't return to the risk register.
whyNot.3: Issues have already happened, so they aren't scored for probability.

B.q: Why is an issue's impact assessed BEFORE it is escalated?
options: So the sponsor never needs to be involved
So the issue can be closed before it is seen
So the sponsor can decide with the facts
So a probability can be added to the log
B.why: Assessment gives the sponsor the impact and options needed to agree a good resolution quickly.

whyNot.0: An issue is beyond tolerance, so the sponsor must be involved.
whyNot.1: Hiding an issue defeats the purpose of escalation.
whyNot.3: Issues are certain; there is no probability to add.

C.q: On Westbrook Bridge, the PM has logged a failed concrete pour and assessed a five-week delay against a two-week tolerance. What should happen next?
options: Add it to the risk register
C.why: It is logged and assessed, and it breaches tolerance, so the next stage is escalation to the sponsor.

whyNot.1: Tracking to closure follows the agreed resolution, which hasn't happened yet.
whyNot.2: Change control follows an agreed resolution that changes the baseline.
whyNot.3: It has already happened, so it is an issue, not a risk.

C.q: The sponsor agrees to fund a second crew, which moves the approved end date. Which stage must now be applied?
C.why: Moving the approved end date changes the baseline, so change control must be applied.

whyNot.1: The issue was logged at the start.
whyNot.3: Escalation has already happened: that is how the sponsor agreed the fix.

C.q: Which sequence shows the issue resolution stages in the correct order?
options: Log, escalate, assess, agree, track, change control
Assess, log, agree, escalate, change control, track
Log, assess, agree, escalate, track, change control
Log, assess, escalate, agree, change control, track
C.why: Identify and log, assess impact, escalate to the sponsor, agree the resolution, apply change control, track to closure.

whyNot.0: Assessment must come before escalation, and change control before closure.
whyNot.1: You can't assess an issue before it is logged, and escalation comes before agreement.
whyNot.2: The sponsor's agreement follows escalation, not the other way round.

reteach.title: The house extension and the hidden sewer
reteach.question: Digging the foundations for a house extension, the builder hits an old sewer pipe right where the new wall should go. How does the builder deal with it, stage by stage?

blocks.body: The builder notes it in the site diary (log), works out it means three weeks and £4,000 extra (assess), and phones the homeowner because that is over the agreed limit (escalate). Together they choose to reroute the pipe (agree). The new layout goes back to building control for approval because the plans change (change control). Finally the builder checks the work is signed off and notes 'survey for drains first' for next time (track to closure).

blocks.text: Telling the neighbours about the sewer might be polite, but it isn't one of the six stages.

explain.body: First the issue is identified and recorded in the issue log with a description and owner. Then its impact is assessed: what it does to time, cost, quality and scope, and what the options are.

test.q: During which stage is the issue's effect on time, cost and quality worked out?
test.why: Assessing the impact establishes what the issue does to the project's objectives.

whyNot.0: Identifying and logging records the issue; the analysis comes next.
whyNot.2: Agreeing the resolution uses the assessment; it doesn't produce it.
whyNot.3: Tracking follows the fix through to closure.

explain.body: Because an issue breaches the PM's tolerance, it is escalated to the sponsor with the facts and options. Together they agree the resolution, and named people are given the actions.

test.q: At which stage are the actions to fix an issue assigned to named people?
test.why: When the resolution is agreed, the actions needed to carry it out are assigned.

whyNot.0: Escalation takes the issue to the sponsor; the fix isn't chosen yet.
whyNot.1: Logging records the issue and its owner, before any fix is chosen.
whyNot.3: Change control authorises baseline changes caused by the fix.

explain.body: If the agreed resolution changes the approved baseline (scope, schedule or budget), it goes through change control so the change is authorised and the plans are updated.

root.label: Does the fix change the baseline?

test.q: Why does an issue's resolution sometimes pass through change control?
options: To score the issue's probability and impact
To inform stakeholders that the issue exists
To decide whether the issue should be logged
To keep any change to the baseline authorised
test.why: Change control makes sure any change to the approved baseline is assessed, approved and recorded.

whyNot.1: Communication happens, but it isn't the purpose of change control.
whyNot.2: Every issue is logged at stage one, regardless of change control.

explain.h: Track to closure, and the odd one out
explain.body: The final stage follows the actions until the fix is confirmed, closes the issue and captures lessons. 'Share with stakeholders' is not a stage.

items.label: stages in the issue resolution process

test.q: A new PM drafts an issue procedure. Which step should be removed because it is NOT a stage of the issue resolution process?
test.why: Sharing with stakeholders is not one of the stages, even though communication happens throughout.

whyNot.1: Identifying and logging is the first stage.
whyNot.2: Assessing the impact is the second stage.
whyNot.3: Tracking to closure is the final stage.
